title: Trump Mulls DeSantis as Pentagon Chief, Targeting Pete Hegseth’s Exit, CBS Reports
body:
President Donald Trump is reportedly weighing former Florida governor Ron DeSantis as a successor to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a move that could see the Florida Republican ascend to the Pentagon in the final weeks of the outgoing administration. According to a source briefed by CBS News, the White House is exploring whether DeSantis could clear Senate confirmation during the lame‑duck period and assume the post after his gubernatorial term ends on Jan. 5, 2025. The speculation comes as Trump’s team grapples with a bruising midterm election that saw Republicans lose control of the House and make modest gains in the Senate, prompting a reassessment of key cabinet positions.

The idea of installing DeSantis—a rising star in the Republican Party and a frequent Trump ally—into the nation’s top civilian defense role would be unprecedented. Historically, former governors have been tapped for cabinet posts, but a sitting governor transitioning directly to the Pentagon is rare, especially given the tight timeline before the inauguration of President‑elect Joe Biden. If Trump proceeds, DeSantis would need to resign the governorship, submit his nomination to the Senate, and secure a majority vote in a chamber now split 50‑50 with Vice President Harris holding the tie‑breaking ballot. The Senate’s foreign‑policy and defense committees would likely scrutinize DeSantis’s limited experience in national security, a factor that could become a focal point in the confirmation hearings.

Political analysts see the maneuver as a calculated gamble. On one hand, placing a high‑profile, Trump‑friendly figure at the Defense Department could cement the former president’s influence over the military establishment during the transition, potentially shaping policy discussions that linger into the next administration. On the other hand, the move risks alienating moderate Republicans and could provoke a contentious confirmation battle. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer has already signaled that any late‑term appointments will be closely examined, especially those that could affect the continuity of defense policy as the United States navigates ongoing challenges in Ukraine, the Indo‑Pacific, and cyber threats.

The internal dynamics of the Trump administration also play a role. Reports indicate that Trump has been consulting advisers and even making direct calls to gauge whether Hegseth should remain in his post. Hegseth, who took office in March 2023, has overseen a period of heightened tension with China and a continued focus on modernizing the force structure. Some senior defense officials have expressed concern that a rapid turnover could disrupt ongoing initiatives, particularly the rollout of the Pentagon’s “Force of the Future” modernization plan. Yet Trump’s pattern of reshuffling cabinet positions to reward loyalty suggests that political considerations may outweigh operational continuity.

For DeSantis, the prospect of a Pentagon appointment presents both opportunity and risk. A successful confirmation would catapult him onto the national stage, positioning him as a potential presidential contender in 2028. However, a failed bid could tarnish his reputation and expose him to criticism for abandoning his gubernatorial duties before the end of his term. Moreover, the timing coincides with a wave of state‑level policy battles in Florida—ranging from education reforms to pandemic response—that have kept DeSantis in the national spotlight. A pivot to a federal role would shift the focus to his stance on defense spending, military procurement, and the ongoing debate over the role of the United States in global conflicts.

As the lame‑duck session unfolds, the Trump administration’s next steps will be closely watched by both Capitol Hill and the Pentagon. Whether DeSantis will be nominated, how the Senate will respond, and what impact the decision will have on the upcoming Biden‑Harris transition remain uncertain. What is clear is that the speculation underscores the lingering influence of the former president on the Republican establishment and highlights the strategic importance of the Defense Department at a moment when the nation faces multiple security challenges. The coming weeks will reveal whether the gambit to place DeSantis at the Pentagon will materialize, and how it will shape the defense agenda as the United States moves into a new political era.
